name: Horsetail extract

card.summary: A silica-rich herbal extract sold for hair and nails, with limited lab data and no single-ingredient hair trials.
card.note: Plant is toxic to livestock; human hair evidence is lacking.

quick.overview:
Horsetail extract comes from a fern-like plant and is promoted in hair supplements and shampoos for its silica content. Its folk use includes strengthening nails.

No human trial of horsetail alone has shown a hair benefit, so its appearance effect is unproven.
quick.mechanism: Lab studies show anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activity in cells. A silica-to-hair pathway is the usual proposal but has not been tested in published human trials.
quick.risks: The plant is toxic to livestock and may form nicotine in polluted conditions. Human safety data for hair-focused use are limited.

lead: Horsetail extract is prepared from Equisetum arvense (field or common horsetail), a perennial fern-like plant native to arctic and temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere.[1] It is marketed in hair, skin and nail supplements, shampoos and nail products as a source of silica, with the plant reported to contain silicon along with flavonoids, saponins, tannins and minerals.[1]

People use it hoping for stronger, thicker-looking hair and firmer nails. The reasoning is the plant's silicon content and its long folk use for strengthening fingernails, as Wikipedia notes, and horsetail appears as one ingredient among many in multi-ingredient hair formulas, such as a 2012 patent filing for an oral hair-condition preparation.[1][5]

Wikipedia describes the evidence for its medicinal properties as limited, with laboratory data suggesting anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antimicrobial and diuretic activity.[1] No published human trial of horsetail alone for hair growth was found; one controlled study tested a nail lacquer containing horsetail with other ingredients, and at least two registered trials have tested multi-ingredient hair supplements.[3][4][8]

chain: Silica is believed to support hair and nail structure
Hair and nails that look stronger and break less
angle.text: Horsetail is taken or applied by people who want stronger-looking hair and nails, on the basis of its silica content and its traditional use for nail strength. It is most often found as one ingredient in hair-and-nail supplements and shampoos rather than alone.

paras: Equisetum arvense spreads by an underground rhizome and produces fertile spore-bearing stems in April and sterile green stems that last through summer; sterile stems are 10 to 90 cm tall.[1] Wikipedia lists silicon, potassium, calcium, manganese, magnesium, phosphorus, phytosterols, vitamins A, E and C, tannins, alkaloids, saponins, flavonoids and glycosides among its constituents, and describes the plant as one that absorbs silicon from soil.[1]

Products use dried shoots in teas and tinctures, standardised extracts in capsules, and extracts in shampoos and nail lacquers. Multi-ingredient oral hair formulas combine horsetail with ingredients such as caffeine, biotin, zinc and others.[5]

Austrian herbal tradition used horsetail tea, baths and compresses for skin, joint, kidney and urinary complaints, Finnish folk medicine valued its silicic acid, and in Iran shoot infusions are believed to help with diabetes and obesity.[1] The plant has historically been used to strengthen fingernails, and to polish pewter and wood because its silica-rich stems are abrasive.[1] Linnaeus described it in 1753, and Japan and Korea eat the spring buds as a vegetable.[1]

Outside personal care, an aqueous extract was approved as a fungicide in the EU, with the review report on it as a basic substance finalised on 20 March 2014, and it is used in biodynamic farming.[1] The plant is classed as an invasive pest in New Zealand.[1]

sections.h: Use in hair and nail products
paras: Horsetail appears in several product formats: shampoos and scalp products, capsules and tinctures taken orally, and ingredient lists of nail lacquers [5][8]. Practitioners of herbal hair care describe it as a silica source, while manufacturers of multi-ingredient formulas pair it with other ingredients, which makes the contribution of any single component hard to separate in the few studies that exist [5][8]. Wikipedia notes that its silicon content is described as 2 to 3 percent, a figure flagged there as needing a citation, and that the plant absorbs silicon from soil, which is unusual among herbs [1].

In the European Union, the herbal medicines committee of the European Medicines Agency published a monograph on Equisetum arvense herb (reference EMA/HMPC/278091/2015) on 17 March 2016. It lists traditional-use indications for minor urinary tract problems, to increase urine output, and for superficial wounds, resting on long use rather than clinical trial evidence; hair and nail uses are not among them [12]. The monograph covers dried aerial parts, expressed juice and extracts, and states that combinations with other herbal substances are not covered [12]. Reported side effects include allergic reactions and, for urinary use, mild gastrointestinal complaints, and the monograph advises against the urinary use where reduced fluid intake is recommended, as in severe heart or kidney disease [12].

A laboratory study of a standardised commercial E. arvense extract reported that it inhibited proliferation and activation of human T lymphocytes in vitro, with reduced IL-2, interferon-gamma and TNF-alpha production, which the authors described as an anti-inflammatory mode of action consistent with its European use for inflammatory disorders.[2] A rat study reported SIRT1-related effects on insulin sensitivity in induced diabetes,[6] and a 2025 rat study examined horsetail and olive extracts against metronidazole-induced pancreatic damage.[7]
Studies outside human health have used horsetail extract on basil plants, in chitosan wound-dressing hydrogels and as a reagent in nanoparticle synthesis.[9][10] None tested hair outcomes.

Wikipedia notes that horsetail is toxic to livestock, particularly horses, and states that the plant may synthesize nicotine under polluted conditions and that other Equisetum species are toxic, in passages the article does not source.[1] No published study tested the safety of oral horsetail products for hair use.

A 2025 qualitative review of online alopecia information lists horsetail extract, along with mineral supplements, biotin, rosemary oil, onion juice and saw palmetto, among alternative remedies touted online that the authors describe as unfounded, and recommends that dermatologists address such claims when they encounter them.[11]
No studies found of horsetail extract on its own for hair loss or hair growth in humans.

A 2009 controlled study in 30 adults with mild to moderate nail psoriasis tested a water-soluble nail lacquer containing hydroxypropyl chitosan, horsetail extract and methylsulphonylmethane, applied daily to the fingernails of the left hand for 24 weeks with the right hand as control. Among 28 analysed patients the NAPSI score fell 65 percent, with 72 percent less pitting, 66 percent less leukonychia and 63 percent less onycholysis in treated nails and no change in untreated nails; no adverse reactions were reported. The product contained several active ingredients and the trial did not isolate the effect of horsetail.[8]

Two registered trials, NCT06841458 (n=45, androgenetic alopecia, started 2024) and NCT06174441 (n=89, hair thinning, started January 2024, completed), test dietary supplements for hair; the registry listings do not establish horsetail as a sole active ingredient, and no results are summarised here.[3][4]

timeline.event: Linnaeus describes Equisetum arvense in Species Plantarum.[1]
EU review report on horsetail as a basic substance finalised; a study of its effects on human lymphocytes is published.[1][2]
The European Medicines Agency's herbal committee publishes a monograph on Equisetum arvense herb for traditional use [12].
Two registered trials of multi-ingredient hair supplements begin.[3][4]

lore.intro: Horsetail is mentioned in hair-supplement marketing and natural-hair discussions mainly as a silica source.

claims.claim: Horsetail silica strengthens hair and supports growth
claims.believers: Proponents of herbal hair care say the plant's silicon content supports hair and nails, echoing its folk use for nail strength.[1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes the evidence for medicinal effects of horsetail as limited, and no published trial has tested horsetail alone for hair; a 2025 review lists it among remedies touted online that the authors call unfounded.[1][11]

claims.believers: Product descriptions say the lacquer strengthens nails and reduces fragility and roughness.[8]
claims.experts: A 24-week controlled study in 30 people with nail psoriasis found improved NAPSI scores in treated nails, but the product contained several active ingredients.[8]
